\chapter{To Have, and How Old You Are}
\label{ch:avoir-age}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use all six forms of avoir, and ask and answer how old someone is the way French does it — by having years rather than being them.}

The verb French leans on hardest, taken one person at a time. Its three singular forms are written ai, as and a and sound the same, which is why French keeps the subject pronouns Spanish drops; its plural endings -ons and -ez survived and are unmistakable. Then the sentence the verb exists for: J'ai vingt ans, \textquotedblleft{}I have twenty years\textquotedblright{}. Never être, and ans cannot be dropped — and every Romance language on the continent agrees while every Germanic one does not.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[j'ai]{j'ai — I have}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-jai}



\begin{quote}
The verb French leans on hardest starts here, with the form you will say most — and it is one sound long.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{elision} — it is \textbf{j'ai}, never \emph{je ai}. Before a vowel \textbf{je} drops its \textbf{e}, the same move that turns \emph{le eau} into \textbf{l'eau}.
  \item The \textbf{ai} is a single vowel, close to English \emph{eh}.
  \item Together: \textbf{j'ai} = \emph{zhay}. One syllable, and the whole of \textquotedblleft{}I have.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{j'ai} is Latin \textbf{habeō}, \textquotedblleft{}I have.\textquotedblright{}

Say those two aloud: \emph{ha-be-o}, then \emph{zhay}. Three syllables become one, and not one consonant of the Latin survives into the vowel.

French does this harder than any of its sisters. Italian kept \textbf{ho}, Spanish kept \textbf{he} — both still a whole syllable with a consonant. French kept a vowel. It is the same appetite that ground \emph{aqua} down to \textbf{eau}, and you will see it again every time a very common word looks like nothing.

The rule of thumb is worth having now: \textbf{the more often a word is said, the more of it wears away.} That is why the most useful words in a language are usually its least recognisable ones.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}j'ai\textquotedblright{} — \emph{zhay}, one syllable
  \item the erosion — \textquotedblleft{}habeō, ho, he, j'ai\textquotedblright{}
  \item a whole sentence — \textquotedblleft{}J'ai un frère\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}I have\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{j'ai}, \emph{zhay}.) Why is it not \emph{je ai}? (\textbf{Elision} — \emph{je} drops its \textbf{e} before a vowel.) What Latin word is it from? (\emph{\textbf{habeō}}.) What do Italian and Spanish still keep that French does not? (A whole \textbf{syllable} — \emph{ho}, \emph{he}.) Next: the same verb, said to one person.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tu as]{tu as — you have}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-as}



\begin{quote}
The second form of the verb, and the first sign that this paradigm is easier to say than it looks to read.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — the \textbf{s} of \textbf{as} is \textbf{not pronounced}.
  \item \textbf{tu as} = \emph{tü ah}. The \textbf{u} of \emph{tu} is the tight front-rounded vowel; the \textbf{as} is a bare open \emph{ah}.
  \item Say \textbf{j'ai} and \textbf{tu as} back to back and notice how little work the verb is doing in either.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{as} is the \textbf{tu} form — the one you use with a friend, a child, or anyone you would call by their first name. It is the same \emph{tu} you met when you learned which \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} to pick.

The written \textbf{s} is a signal to the eye and nothing to the ear. That is the normal state of affairs in French verbs: the endings are alive on the page and almost dead in the mouth. It is why the pronoun is not optional — \emph{as} on its own would tell a listener nothing about who has something.

Keep that in mind as the paradigm fills in. You are learning six written forms and rather fewer sounds.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tu as\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tü ah}, the \emph{s} silent
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as\textquotedblright{}
  \item with a noun — \textquotedblleft{}Tu as un frère\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}you have\textquotedblright{} to a friend? (\textbf{tu as}, \emph{tü ah}.) Is the \textbf{s} pronounced? (\textbf{No.}) Why can you not drop the pronoun? (The verb form alone \textbf{does not say who} — the pronoun carries it.) Next: he and she.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[il a, elle a]{il a, elle a — he has, she has}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-a}



\begin{quote}
The third form, and the shortest verb you will ever meet: one letter.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a} is a bare open \emph{ah} — the same sound as \textbf{tu as}, with nothing written after it.
  \item \textbf{il a} = \emph{eel ah}. \textbf{elle a} = \emph{el ah}.
  \item All three singular forms are now in your mouth, and the next lesson is about what they have in common.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{a} is the form for \textbf{il} (he) and \textbf{elle} (she), and it is a single letter carrying an entire verb.

You already know the two pronouns from the articles: \textbf{le} and \textbf{la} split the world into masculine and feminine, and \textbf{il} and \textbf{elle} do the same for people. French has no separate word for \emph{it} — a table is \emph{elle}, a book is \emph{il}, because the noun's gender decides.

One thing to notice for later. When French turns this into a question by putting the verb first, two vowels would collide — \emph{a il ?} — so a \textbf{t} is pushed in between them: \textbf{a-t-il ?}, \textquotedblleft{}has he?\textquotedblright{} That \textbf{t} means nothing at all. It is there purely so the mouth has something to land on.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}il a, elle a\textquotedblright{} — \emph{eel ah}, \emph{el ah}
  \item the three singulars — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as, il a\textquotedblright{}
  \item the question shape — \textquotedblleft{}a-t-il ?\textquotedblright{}; the \emph{t} is only there for the mouth
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}he has\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{il a}.) And \textquotedblleft{}she has\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{elle a}.) How many letters is the verb? (\textbf{One.}) What is the \textbf{t} doing in \emph{a-t-il ?} (\textbf{Nothing} — it keeps two vowels from colliding.) Next: why those three forms are harder to hear than to read.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai · as · a]{ai · as · a — three spellings, one ear}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-ai-as-a}



\begin{quote}
You have the three singular forms. Say them one after another and listen to how much difference there actually is.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the endings are for the eye}]
Written, the three singular forms are \textbf{ai}, \textbf{as}, \textbf{a} — three different words. Spoken, \textbf{as} and \textbf{a} are the same bare \emph{ah}, and \textbf{ai} is a single vowel too. The written endings differ; your ear has almost nothing to work with.

This is not a quirk of \emph{avoir}. It is the central fact about French verbs, and it has one large consequence: \textbf{the pronoun is compulsory.}

Spanish can say \emph{tengo} and drop the \emph{yo}, because \emph{-o} means \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} out loud. French cannot drop the \emph{je}, because the ending that would have carried it went silent centuries ago. So French kept the pronoun and Spanish did not, and the two languages ended up in different places for the same reason: \textbf{what the ear can still hear decides what the sentence must carry.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three verb forms bare — \textquotedblleft{}ai, as, a\textquotedblright{}; hear how close they are
  \item them with their pronouns — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as, il a\textquotedblright{}
  \item the consequence — \textquotedblleft{}the pronoun does the work the ending stopped doing\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as, il a\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write the three singular forms. (\textbf{ai}, \textbf{as}, \textbf{a}.) How many distinct sounds are there? (Effectively \textbf{one} — a bare vowel.) Why can French not drop its subject pronouns the way Spanish can? (Because the \textbf{endings are silent} — the pronoun is the only thing left that says \textbf{who}.) Next: the plural, where the endings come back to life.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nous avons]{nous avons — we have}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-avons}



\begin{quote}
Three forms that sound alike, and then this: an ending you can actually hear.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{nous avons} = \emph{noo-za-VO(N)}. The \textbf{s} of \emph{nous} wakes up and buzzes into the vowel — that is the liaison you already know.
  \item \texttt{nasal-on} — the \textbf{-ons} ending is a nasal vowel; the \textbf{n} is the nose, not a consonant.
  \item Weight on the last syllable, as almost always in French.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{avons} is Latin \textbf{habēmus}, \textquotedblleft{}we have.\textquotedblright{}

Here the paradigm turns around. The three singular endings wore away to nothing; \textbf{-ons} did not. It is a full syllable, it is unmistakable, and it belongs to \textbf{nous} and nothing else.

That pattern holds across French verbs: \textbf{-ons} for \emph{nous}, \textbf{-ez} for \emph{vous}. Once you have those two you can hear the plural coming in any verb in the language, regular or not. \emph{avoir} is one of the most irregular verbs French has, and it still obeys this.

So the difficulty is not spread evenly. The singular is a listening problem and the plural is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nous avons\textquotedblright{} — \emph{noo-za-VO(N)}, the \emph{s} buzzing across
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}il a\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}nous avons\textquotedblright{}; one is a vowel, one is a syllable
  \item the ending alone — \textquotedblleft{}-ons is always nous\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}we have\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{nous avons}, \emph{noo-za-VO(N)}.) Which ending marks \emph{nous}? (\textbf{-ons}.) Why is this form easier to hear than \emph{il a}? (The \textbf{plural endings survived} where the singular ones went silent.) Next: the other you.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vous avez]{vous avez — you have}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-avez}



\begin{quote}
The second plural ending, and a form you will use with strangers far more often than with crowds.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{vous avez} = \emph{voo-za-VAY}. The same buzzing liaison as \emph{nous avons}.
  \item \texttt{vowel-e-acute} — the \textbf{-ez} is the bright, narrow \emph{ay} of \textbf{février}. The \textbf{z} is silent.
  \item Say \textbf{nous avons, vous avez} together: \emph{-ons}, \emph{-ez}, the two plural endings of nearly every French verb.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{avez} is Latin \textbf{habētis}, and it goes with \textbf{vous}.

\textbf{vous} is two things at once. It is the plural \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — several people. And it is the polite \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} for \textbf{one} person, which is the use you will need first and most: a shopkeeper, a stranger, anyone you have not been invited to call \emph{tu}.

So \emph{vous avez} is what you say to one person you are being careful with. Getting this wrong is one of the few grammar mistakes in French that a listener hears as a mistake about \textbf{them} rather than about the language, which is why \emph{tu} and \emph{vous} is worth more attention than most endings.

The verb form does not change between the two meanings. Only who you are looking at does.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vous avez\textquotedblright{} — \emph{voo-za-VAY}
  \item the two plural endings — \textquotedblleft{}nous avons, vous avez\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two jobs — \textquotedblleft{}vous to a group, vous to one stranger\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}you have\textquotedblright{} politely? (\textbf{vous avez}, \emph{voo-za-VAY}.) What are the two jobs \emph{vous} does? (\textbf{Plural you}, and \textbf{polite you} to one person.) Which ending marks \emph{vous}? (\textbf{-ez}.) Next: the last form, and the odd one.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ils ont, elles ont]{ils ont, elles ont — they have}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-ont}



\begin{quote}
The sixth and last form, and the one that does not resemble the other five.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ils ont} = \emph{eel-ZO(N)}. The \textbf{s} of \emph{ils} buzzes across into the vowel.
  \item \texttt{nasal-on} — \textbf{ont} is one nasal vowel; the \textbf{n} and \textbf{t} are both silent.
  \item \textbf{elles ont} = \emph{el-ZO(N)}, identical but for the first vowel.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ont} is Latin \textbf{habent}, and it is the odd one out: every other form of \emph{avoir} has an \textbf{a} in it, and this one does not.

There is a trap here worth meeting before you fall into it. \textbf{ils ont} is \textquotedblleft{}they have.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{ils sont} is \textquotedblleft{}they \textbf{are}.\textquotedblright{} One consonant apart, and both extremely common. The way to keep them apart is the liaison: \emph{ils \textbf{ont}} buzzes — \emph{eel-\textbf{z}-o(n)} — while \emph{ils \textbf{sont}} hisses, \emph{eel \textbf{s}o(n)}. The buzz means \emph{have}.

That is the whole paradigm. Six forms, and you now have all of them:

\textbf{j'ai · tu as · il a · nous avons · vous avez · ils ont}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ils ont\textquotedblright{} — \emph{eel-ZO(N)}, the buzz
  \item the trap — \textquotedblleft{}ils ont\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}ils sont\textquotedblright{}; buzz means have
  \item all six in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}they have\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{ils ont}, \emph{eel-ZO(N)}.) What does \emph{ils sont} mean instead? (\textbf{They are.}) How do you tell them apart by ear? (\textbf{ils ont} buzzes; \textbf{ils sont} hisses.) What is unusual about \emph{ont} among the six forms? (It is the only one with \textbf{no a} in it.) Next: where the whole verb came from.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[habēre]{habēre — the root you already met}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-habere}



\begin{quote}
You have all six forms of \emph{avoir}. You have also, without being told, already learned its root — in a different verb, several chapters ago.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{avoir} is Latin \textbf{habēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to have.\textquotedblright{}

Now recall \textbf{habiter}, \textquotedblleft{}to live somewhere.\textquotedblright{} That is Latin \textbf{habitāre} — and \emph{habitāre} is just \emph{habēre} run through a pattern that means \textquotedblleft{}keep doing it.\textquotedblright{} To \emph{habitāre} a place is to \textbf{keep having} it.

So \emph{avoir} and \emph{habiter} are the same verb twice: one wore down to a vowel, the other kept the \emph{h}, the \emph{b} and the \emph{t} because it was said far less often. The two French verbs sitting at opposite ends of the same root are a compact demonstration of the rule you met with \emph{j'ai}: frequency is what erodes a word.

English borrowed the Latin whole and shows the root undisguised every time:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{habit} — what you \emph{have} regularly
  \item \textbf{inhabit} — to \emph{have} a place; the exact twin of \emph{habiter}
  \item \textbf{exhibit} — to \emph{hold} out
  \item \textbf{prohibit} — to \emph{hold} back
\end{itemize}

Four English words, one French verb you use constantly, and one French verb you met learning to say where you live — all the same handful of Latin letters.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the root — \textquotedblleft{}habēre\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two French verbs — \textquotedblleft{}avoir, habiter\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English four — \textquotedblleft{}habit, inhabit, exhibit, prohibit\textquotedblright{}
  \item the twins — \textquotedblleft{}habiter, inhabit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin verb is \emph{avoir} from? (\emph{\textbf{habēre}}.) Which other French verb you already know comes from it? (\emph{\textbf{habiter}} — from \emph{habitāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep having a place\textquotedblright{}.) Which English word is \emph{habiter}'s exact twin? (\textbf{inhabit}.) Why did \emph{avoir} wear down so much further than \emph{habiter}? (It is said \textbf{far more often} — frequency erodes a word.) Next: all six forms, together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the whole of avoir}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-practice-avoir}



\begin{quote}
Six forms, learned one at a time. This is the first time they stand together — and a paradigm you have already built is a recap, not a wall.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the six in order}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont\textquotedblright{}
  \item the singulars alone — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as, il a\textquotedblright{}
  \item the plurals alone — \textquotedblleft{}nous avons, vous avez, ils ont\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: the two halves sound different}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three that blur — \textquotedblleft{}ai, as, a\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two that do not — \textquotedblleft{}-ons, -ez\textquotedblright{}
  \item the trap — \textquotedblleft{}ils ont, ils sont\textquotedblright{}; buzz for have, hiss for are
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: use it}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}J'ai un frère\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tu as une sœur\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Nous avons du pain\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root — \textquotedblleft{}avoir, habiter, inhabit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built so far}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{six forms} of the verb French leans on hardest, one lesson each.
  \item \textbf{a listening fact} — the singular endings are silent, so French keeps its subject pronouns where Spanish drops them.
  \item \textbf{a root that pays twice} — \emph{habēre} gave French \emph{avoir} and \emph{habiter}, and English \emph{habit}, \emph{inhabit}, \emph{exhibit}, \emph{prohibit}.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give all six forms without stopping. Which three sound effectively the same? (\textbf{ai, as, a}.) Which two endings can you always hear? (\textbf{-ons} and \textbf{-ez}.) How do you hear the difference between \emph{ils ont} and \emph{ils sont}? (The \textbf{buzz} — \emph{ont} takes a liaison \textbf{z}, \emph{sont} hisses.) What Latin verb is behind all of it? (\emph{\textbf{habēre}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[un an, des ans]{un an — a year}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-an}



\begin{quote}
One small word, and it unlocks the single most common question anyone will ask you in a new language.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-an} — \textbf{an} is a \textbf{nasal vowel}, the same one in \textbf{blanc} and \textbf{janvier}. The \textbf{n} is the nose, not a consonant.
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — the plural \textbf{ans} adds a written \textbf{s} and no sound at all.
  \item \textbf{un an} = \emph{a(n)-NA(N)}: the \textbf{n} of \emph{un} links across into the vowel.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{an} is Latin \textbf{annus}, \textquotedblleft{}year,\textquotedblright{} and English kept it whole in a whole shelf of words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{annual} — happening each year
  \item \textbf{anniversary} — literally the year \textbf{turning} (\emph{annus} + \emph{vertere}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{annals} — a record kept year by year
  \item \emph{\textbf{per annum}} — English never even translated this one
\end{itemize}

You have met \emph{annus}'s neighbours already: the months came out of the same Roman calendar, and \emph{janvier} stands at the door of exactly this word.

French also has a second word for year, \textbf{année}, and the difference is real but small: \emph{an} counts years, \emph{année} describes them as a stretch of time. For counting — which is what the next lesson does — you want \textbf{an}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un an\textquotedblright{} — \emph{a(n)-NA(N)}, both vowels through the nose
  \item the plural — \textquotedblleft{}deux ans, dix ans\textquotedblright{}; the \emph{s} is silent
  \item the English family — \textquotedblleft{}annual, anniversary, annals\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}a year\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{un an}.) What Latin word is it? (\emph{\textbf{annus}}.) Does the plural \textbf{ans} sound different from \textbf{an}? (\textbf{No} — the \textbf{s} is silent.) What does \emph{anniversary} literally say? (The \textbf{year turning}.) Next: what French does with \emph{avoir} and \emph{ans} together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[j'ai vingt ans]{j'ai vingt ans — having your years}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-jai-vingt-ans}



\begin{quote}
Here is the first thing French lets you say that English cannot say the same way at all.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: age is something you have}]
English \textbf{is} its age: \emph{I am twenty}. French \textbf{has} it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{J'ai vingt ans.} — literally, \textquotedblleft{}I \emph{have} twenty years.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Two things follow, and both are absolute.

\textbf{The verb is \emph{avoir}, never \emph{être}.} \emph{Je suis vingt ans} is not a stylistic choice; it is simply wrong, and it is the single most common thing an English speaker gets wrong in their first month.

\textbf{And \emph{ans} cannot be dropped.} English says \textquotedblleft{}I'm twenty\textquotedblright{} with no noun at all. French must name the years: \emph{J'ai vingt} on its own means nothing.

One sound to get right. \textbf{vingt} normally ends in silence — you learned it as \emph{VA(N)}, with the \textbf{g} and \textbf{t} both dead. Put \textbf{ans} after it and the \textbf{t} \textbf{wakes up}: \emph{vin-\textbf{t}-a(n)}. That is liaison, doing what it always does — reviving a buried consonant when a vowel follows it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}J'ai vingt ans\textquotedblright{} — with the liaison, \emph{vin-t-a(n)}
  \item the rule — \textquotedblleft{}avoir, never être\textquotedblright{}
  \item the buried t waking — \textquotedblleft{}vingt\textquotedblright{} alone, then \textquotedblleft{}vingt ans\textquotedblright{}
  \item your own age, with the numbers you have
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}J'ai vingt ans\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does French say \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{J'ai vingt ans} — \textquotedblleft{}I \emph{have} twenty years\textquotedblright{}.) Which verb, and which is wrong? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}}; \emph{\textbf{être}} is wrong.) Can you drop \emph{ans} the way English drops \textquotedblleft{}years\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No.}) What happens to the \textbf{t} of \emph{vingt} before \emph{ans}? (It \textbf{wakes up} — \emph{vin-t-a(n)}, a liaison.) Next: how to ask.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Quel âge as-tu ?]{Quel âge as-tu ? — asking someone's age}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-quel-age}



\begin{quote}
You can answer the question. Now you can ask it — and this is a phrase worth taking whole rather than building.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Quel âge as-tu ?} = \emph{kel AHZH ah-tü}.
  \item \texttt{circumflex} — the hat on \textbf{â} is the gravestone you met on \textbf{août}: it marks a lost \textbf{s}. Older French wrote \emph{aage}, and before that Latin had \emph{aetāticum}.
  \item The \textbf{g} of \emph{âge} is the soft \emph{zh} of \textbf{rouge}.
  \item The polite form is \textbf{Quel âge avez-vous ?} — \emph{kel AHZH ah-vay-VOO}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Take it as one unit, the way you took \emph{Comment vous appelez-vous ?}

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Quel âge as-tu ?} — \textquotedblleft{}What age do you \emph{have}?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{J'ai vingt ans.} — \textquotedblleft{}I \emph{have} twenty years.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Notice the question uses \textbf{avoir} as well. The whole exchange is built on having, on both sides — which is what makes it a pair worth memorising together rather than two separate facts.

And \textbf{âge} is a word you already own in English. \emph{Age} came into English from French, hat and all, having lost its \emph{s} on the way: Latin \emph{aetāticum} $\to$ \emph{aage} $\to$ \textbf{âge} $\to$ English \textbf{age}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Quel âge as-tu ?\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kel AHZH ah-tü}
  \item the polite one — \textquotedblleft{}Quel âge avez-vous ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item both halves — \textquotedblleft{}Quel âge as-tu ? J'ai vingt ans.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the hat's meaning — \textquotedblleft{}â marks a lost s, like août\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Quel âge as-tu ? J'ai vingt ans.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask a friend their age? (\textbf{Quel âge as-tu ?}) And a stranger? (\textbf{Quel âge avez-vous ?}) Which verb does the \textbf{question} use? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}} — the same as the answer.) What does the circumflex on \textbf{â} mark? (A \textbf{lost s}.) Next: who else in Europe does it this way.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[j'ai vingt ans / I am twenty]{\textquotedblleft{}having\textquotedblright{} your years — who else does it}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-avoir-etre-langues}



\begin{quote}
French is not being strange here. It is on one side of a line that runs straight across Europe, and the line is exactly where you would draw it.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
Ask the same question in six languages and count the verbs.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I am 20\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{verb} \\
\midrule
French & \emph{j'ai vingt ans} & have \\
Spanish & \emph{tengo veinte años} & have \\
Italian & \emph{ho venti anni} & have \\
Portuguese & \emph{tenho vinte anos} & have \\
German & \emph{ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt} & be \\
English & \emph{I am twenty} & be \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A clean split, and not a coincidental one: every \textbf{Romance} language on that list \emph{has} its years, and every \textbf{Germanic} one \emph{is} them.

French treats age as something you \textbf{carry}: a count of years in your possession, which grows. English treats it as something you \textbf{are}, a property like tall or tired.

Neither is more logical. What matters is that the choice is inherited rather than reasoned: French did not decide this, it received it, along with the rest of what Latin left behind. And it means the mistake you are most likely to make — \emph{je suis vingt ans} — is you importing your own family's habit into another one.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four that have — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tengo, ho, tenho\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two that are — \textquotedblleft{}ich bin, I am\textquotedblright{}
  \item the line — \textquotedblleft{}Romance has its years; Germanic is its years\textquotedblright{}
  \item the French one again, correctly — \textquotedblleft{}J'ai vingt ans\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language family uses \textbf{have} for age? (\textbf{Romance} — French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese.) Which uses \textbf{be}? (\textbf{Germanic} — German, English.) Is either one more logical? (\textbf{No} — the choice is \textbf{inherited}, not reasoned.) Which error does that make an English speaker likely to commit? (\emph{\textbf{Je suis vingt ans}} — importing English's \emph{be}.) Next: all of it together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — to have, and how old you are}

\label{lesson:FR-C14-practice}



\begin{quote}
A verb and a sentence. Run the verb first, then use it for the thing it will earn its keep on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the paradigm, cold}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont\textquotedblright{}
  \item backwards — \textquotedblleft{}ils ont, vous avez, nous avons, il a, tu as, j'ai\textquotedblright{}
  \item the trap — \textquotedblleft{}ils ont, ils sont\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: the exchange}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Quel âge as-tu ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}J'ai vingt ans\textquotedblright{} — with the liaison, \emph{vin-t-a(n)}
  \item the polite pair — \textquotedblleft{}Quel âge avez-vous ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item your own age
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: use the verb on what you own}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}J'ai un frère, j'ai une sœur\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Nous avons du pain et du vin\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root pair — \textquotedblleft{}avoir, habiter\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{the whole of \emph{avoir}}, six forms, one lesson each, and a paradigm you built rather than one you were handed.
  \item \textbf{why French keeps its pronouns} — the singular endings went silent, so \emph{je}, \emph{tu} and \emph{il} carry what the verb stopped saying.
  \item \textbf{age is something you have} — \emph{J'ai vingt ans}, never \emph{je suis}, and \emph{ans} is compulsory. Every Romance language on the continent agrees with French, and every Germanic one disagrees.
  \item \textbf{one root, two verbs, four English words} — \emph{habēre} gave \emph{avoir} and \emph{habiter}, plus \emph{habit}, \emph{inhabit}, \emph{exhibit}, \emph{prohibit}.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the six forms of \emph{avoir}. Ask a friend their age. (\textbf{Quel âge as-tu ?}) Answer with your own. Which verb must you never use for age? (\emph{\textbf{être}}.) Can \emph{ans} be left out? (\textbf{No.}) Which other French verb shares \emph{avoir}'s root? (\emph{\textbf{habiter}}.) How do you hear \emph{ils ont} against \emph{ils sont}? (The \textbf{buzz} against the \textbf{hiss}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
